question: A fast/slow servo stroke now compiles to three states (MAM-command state exiting on MAM.IP, transition-band wait state exiting on {Pos}Transition.InPosWide, MCD speed-change state exiting on strict arrival). proposedSolution: My proposal: two rungs per stroke — the MAM-command state and the MCD state share the destination-arrival alarm ("Waiting For {Axis} To Reach {Target} Position") because both are waiting on the same final move, and the transition-band wait states get their own "...To Reach {Target} Speed Transition" rung. That keeps every message naming the milestone the state is actually waiting on. Do you like this, or do you want one alarm rung per state?

answer: Answered by verified v7 R20: two alarms per stroke - the MAM-command state and the MCD state share the destination-arrival alarm (Alarm[2] Reach Pick = states 7+13, Alarm[3] Reach Place = 31+37, Alarm[4] Reach Retract = 19+25+43+49+100), and the transition-band wait states get their own per-transition-point alarm shared by both directions (Alarm[6] Pick Speed Transition = 10+22, Alarm[7] Place Speed Transition = 34+46). question: Where does the boundary sit for shared part-tracking data — may a station program write the tracking record and another program's Control members, or must all cross-program effects go through a defined interface?

question: For pass/fail inspection or verify stations, is the consecutive-failure counter the ONLY alarm shape — i.e. a single failed part never raises an alarm at all, it just writes Failure into part tracking and rides to the reject station — or are there conditions where the first failure should fault the machine?
proposedSolution: Treat the consecutive-failure counter as the standard and only per-part alarm shape: an individual failure is DATA (Failure + FailureType into the nest, counted by StationPerformance, routed to the reject unload), not a machine condition, because stopping on one bad part contradicts 'machines that stop less' and the reject path already handles it. Raise a fault only when the run of failures says the MACHINE is wrong rather than the part — ConsecFails.Setpoint, with the alarm clearing its own counter so the operator gets one fault per run, not one per part. The exceptions I would carve out are conditions that are not part quality at all but station integrity discovered by the same sensors (both sensors made when only one can be, a sensor stuck for N consecutive indexes regardless of result, or a failure at a station whose failure mode risks damage downstream) — those fault on first occurrence because waiting for a run of them just makes more scrap.

question: Which station conditions are supposed to raise q_Pause to the indexer versus simply holding in the station's own wait state? The template wires q_Pause straight off the 'Waiting For Part Present' warning on the load/PNP stations, but any station wait effectively stalls the dial anyway via q_StationComplete.
proposedSolution: My reading: q_Pause is not 'I am busy', it is 'I am STARVED and no amount of dial time fixes it' — a station that is merely mid-motion holds q_StationComplete low and the indexer waits in state 4 with its normal alarm coverage, which is the right behavior for a wait that will end on its own. q_Pause exists to change the MACHINE's posture for a wait that will not end on its own: it is raised off the Severity-1 starvation warning, it carries a PauseReason so the HMI can say which station is starved, it moves the indexer into dedicated states 40/42 (so the pause is visible in state history and gets its own 2000 ms restart transition rather than a jerky restart), and it drives the Production program's paused-minutes bucket so OEE separates starvation from downtime. So the rule I would apply: raise q_Pause exactly where you raise a Severity-1 starvation/upstream warning, never for an in-progress motion, and always with a distinct PauseReason code.

question: Are Fanuc UI commands (Start, RemoteStart, CycleStop, FaultReset) always to be driven through the 250 ms flasher rather than a one-shot or a held bit, and is the same pulsing expected for other robot brands' remote-start channels?
proposedSolution: Treat flasher-pulsing as the standard for edge-triggered robot UI inputs: the Fanuc controller latches these on a rising edge but scan-length pulses can be missed across the EtherNet/IP update, and a held bit blocks re-issue after a failed attempt. The 250 ms flasher gives a repeating, self-retrying edge that clears itself when the gating state exits — which is why the exemplar also keeps a 'Robot Program Did Not Start' timeout alarm on those same states rather than relying on one attempt. For other brands, keep the pulse where the vendor documents an edge-triggered input, and hold the bit where the vendor documents a level (as with IMSTP/SFSPD/Enable here).

question: For a continuously-running utility machine (a conveyor group with no per-part cycle), is a single long-lived 'Running' state plus staged start/stop states the intended shape, and what should its cycle timer and OEE contribution be?

question: Is `AOI_FanucRecipe` (prepare-command → echo → recipe number → echo → Success, 10 s timeout) the standard mechanism for robot program/part-family selection, and must recipe change always be blocked while the machine is running?

question: The Chassis mechanism program ships with NO lockout 99 and NO init block 100–124 (Initialized is hard-off), and faults in two stages (76 stop all motion → 79 disable servos → 127). Does that generalize — i.e. is 'a program that owns a MECHANISM rather than a part omits lockout/init and uses a staged fault stop' the rule, with 99/100–124 reserved for part-handling stations?
proposedSolution: Yes: lockout 99 exists so a station can be skipped in the part flow, and init 100–124 exists to resolve a part-in-hand posture — a mechanism that carries no part has neither, so its 'init' is whatever re-establishes the mechanism's own sync (resync, engaging camming) and belongs in the sequence because it needs moves that are only lawful before camming. The staged fault stop is the general rule wherever motion must be STOPPED before drives are disabled (cammed pairs, vertical loads): 127 stays the terminal faulted state, with the stop/disable steps as their own numbered states carrying their own timeout alarms.

question: Chassis_CamPos_Check's timing advance (parabolic, SQRT(0.865·v − 86.5)° above 100 deg/s) is enabled per call. Is 'advance ON for actuator commands, OFF for sensor reads' the intended rule, and where does the 0.865/86.5 curve come from — is it a fixed SDC constant or per-machine tuning?
proposedSolution: Yes on the rule: an output has response time (valve shift + cylinder travel), so its trigger must lead the target angle more as the machine speeds up in order to act at the same physical place; a read has no actuation delay and wants the true angle, so advance stays off (and the shipped stations do exactly that — gripper/vacuum engage-disengage use 1, probe checks use 0). Treat the curve constants as a fixed template calibration (zero advance below 100 deg/s, growing as the square root of speed) and do not re-derive them per job; if a machine's valves are unusually slow, adjust the station's engage/disengage angle rather than the AOI.

question: When a retry ladder escalates across state machines — the pick/strip SM exhausts its retries and the recovery is 'index the dial to the next stack' — who owns the escalation state: the consumer SM (a side-path excursion that requests a new source) or the indexer SM (a search-index mode)?

Neither reaches into the other's devices; the request/on-station-qualified handshake pair is the whole coupling.

question: What is the intended use of AlarmData.DoNotSaveToHistory — is it reserved for standing status-type warnings (Bypass, lockout) so history stays a record of events rather than states, or is it also used for high-chatter device alarms?
proposedSolution: Treat it as for standing status-type entries only (Bypass active, station locked out, maintenance mode): conditions that must annunciate continuously but have no event value and would otherwise fill p_History with one long-duration entry per shift. Chattering device alarms should stay in history — their Count/Duration is exactly what TopAlarms needs to expose the nuisance; fix the chatter with the seal-in-until-reset rung shape instead of hiding it.

question: p_Active is dimensioned 16 and rung 13 is unrolled over exactly those 16 slots. Is 16 the fixed machine-wide ceiling on CONCURRENTLY active alarms, and what does the ProgramAlarmHandler do when a 17th alarm latches — drop it, or overwrite?
proposedSolution: Treat 16 as a real design budget on simultaneous active alarms, not on total alarm definitions: the handler publishes only currently-active entries into p_Active, and once full, later alarms are not published, so they never appear on the popup and can never be named AlarmStop. Practical guidance: keep swarm-style rungs (one per partner, one per sensor) composed into a single message rather than separate indices, and if a machine plausibly exceeds 16 at once, raise it with the leads before growing the array — rung 13's unrolled branches and the COP fan-out in rung 5 must be extended in lockstep.
context: Machine alarm spine capacity — from Alarms.L5X R01_Logic rungs 5 and 13

question: The popup-90 force is gated on faults only, so a Severity-1 warning never raises the alarm screen. Is any operator annunciation of warnings expected (banner, lamp, andon) or is the warning list purely pull-based on screen 91?
proposedSolution: Read it as intentional: warnings pause or inform but must not seize the operator's screen mid-task, so they are pull-based on the all-alarms screen plus whatever stacklight/andon the Supervisor drives from q_WarningActive. Since a warning also holds the auto-close of the fault popup, the operator does get told at the moment it matters — after a fault clears the screen stays up until the warning is dealt with too.

question: Is an alarm's identity for HMI/reporting purposes truly the ProgramID+AlarmID pair, or does any faceplate/report key on AlarmID alone? It decides whether AlarmIDs are per-program-scoped (every station starting at Alarm[0]) or must be globally unique.
proposedSolution: Treat it as per-program scoped: the AOI takes PublicProgramIDTag as an InOut and stamps every published entry with it (echoing MyProgramID), and Group is the filter field — so the composite ProgramID+AlarmID is the key and stations can all index from Alarm[0]. I've flagged the older 'never reuse an AlarmID' note in alarms.md as a CONFLICT pending a ruling, in case an HMI object keys on AlarmID alone.

question: How is each program's PublicProgramIDTag value assigned — station number, import order, or a project-wide registry — and who owns keeping them unique?
proposedSolution: Convention appears to be the station number (S03_PartLoad = 3, S05_ServoPNP = 5) with the machine-level Alarms program stamping 0, set once as the program's public INT and read back through MyProgramID for the HMI. Uniqueness is hand-maintained by the CE adding the program — the same manual step as adding the XIO to the \Alarms roll-up rungs 2 and 4, so both edits should be done in one pass.

question: Does anything in the standard consume AlarmData.Group, and if so what are the agreed group numbers? If it is purely an HMI filter we should say so explicitly so station rungs stop leaving it at 0 by accident (or stop inventing values).
proposedSolution: Treat Group as an HMI/report filter only — the handler stamps identity from ProgramID+AlarmID and the blame scan in \Alarms R13 keys on .Active and Severity, never on Group. Default it to 0 (unclassified) in station rungs unless a project's HMI defines a group list (e.g. 1=safety, 2=servo, 3=pneumatic, 4=material supply); if a project does define one, MOVE it in the same rung as the Severity move so the classification travels with the alarm.

question: Is DoNotSaveToHistory intended to be set once at first-scan initialization for the handful of standing status warnings (Bypass, Lockout notice), or asserted in the alarm rung itself each scan?
proposedSolution: Set it once in the station's initialization/first-scan rung for the specific Alarm[i] slots that are standing status indications, not in the alarm rung. It is a property of the alarm slot, not of the event, and keeping it out of the condition rung leaves that rung single-purpose (condition + seal + message + FaultTime). Since the bit rides inside the record under COP, an init-time set survives every publish and history copy.

question: Since TopAlarmsDT/AlarmHistory store the message as a plain STRING (82 chars) while AlarmData carries STRING100, should we treat 82 as the hard authoring ceiling for all alarm text — i.e. budget the station prefix + condition so a composed offender suffix still lands inside 82?
proposedSolution: Yes — author to 82. The record may hold 100, but anything past 82 is invisible in history and the top-5, and two long messages sharing their first 82 characters collapse into one statistics bucket. Practical budget: keep the fixed prefix+condition under ~60 characters so a CONCATenated offender name (" - S05 Servo PNP") still survives; put the discriminating token early rather than at the tail.

question: Does the operator Reset input clear both TopAlarms and TopShiftAlarms, and do the per-shift buckets accumulate across days until reset (chronic shift pattern) or zero at each shift rollover (today-only view)?
proposedSolution: Read the two InOuts as two independent windows: Reset is the campaign zero and should clear both lists so the Pareto and the per-shift breakdown always describe the same period; the per-shift buckets then accumulate by shift number across days, which is what exposes a chronic 3rd-shift problem. If a plant wants a today-only view, that is an HMI-driven Reset at shift change, not extra PLC logic — p_History remains the untouched audit trail either way. Worth confirming with Dan which behavior the AOI actually implements before we document it as mechanism.

question: Does the standard OEE AOI compute Availability as RunTime/PlannedProductionTime or as (PlannedProductionTime - Downtime)/PlannedProductionTime — i.e. is Downtime an input to the math or only carried for reporting? Those differ whenever a machine is idle-but-not-faulted.
proposedSolution: Treat RunTime/PlannedProductionTime as the authoritative Availability and use Downtime as the fault-attributed loss for reporting/Pareto. That keeps Availability honest when a machine is starved or paused (idle time still costs availability, but isn't blamed on a fault), and keeps Downtime consistent with the standard's fault-only downtime rule. Until confirmed, drive both inputs from the same accounting so the two formulas agree.

question: What time unit do the DINT time inputs expect? IdealCycleTime is REAL seconds, but ProductionData exposes both ElapsedSec and ElapsedMin — a mixed feed silently scales Performance by 60.
proposedSolution: Standardize on seconds for all three DINT inputs (feed the ElapsedSec-family tags) since IdealCycleTime is in seconds, and convert to minutes only for HMI display. Recommend the AOI description/HMI faceplate state the unit explicitly, and that Performance be sanity-checked at commissioning (a value near 1.7% or 6000% is the classic seconds/minutes mix-up).

question: Should Performance be clamped at 100% (and IdealCycleTime re-baselined) when a machine beats its ideal cycle, or is >100% intentionally left visible?
proposedSolution: Leave it unclamped so >100% is visible as a signal that IdealCycleTime is stale, but treat a sustained >100% as an action item to re-baseline the constant from the debug speed-ramp result. Clamping hides performance loss elsewhere in the shift; a visible 104% prompts the engineer to fix the constant instead of trusting a flattering OEE.

question: Which fast/slow servo stroke shape is the standard one — the template's two states (MAM state exiting on MAM.IP + the DESTINATION RangeCheck's wide deadband, then the MCD state) sharing ONE destination-arrival alarm, or v7's three states with a separately taught {Pos}Transition RangeCheck and its own 'Waiting For ... Speed Transition' alarm?
proposedSolution: Default to the TEMPLATE shape: two states, the speed change triggered off the destination's wide deadband, one alarm per taught position per axis (Alarm[2] covering states 7+10, Alarm[4] covering 16/19/37/40/100). Treat a separately taught transition point as an application choice reserved for long strokes where the speed change must happen far from the target — and then, and only then, it becomes a real milestone that earns its own alarm rung. Rule of thumb: the alarm list mirrors the POSITION list, so no alarm may exist for a position that is not taught.
context: alarm partitioning / MCD speed-change model — from S05_ServoPNP.L5X

question: Which transitions are exempt from the SS_OK single-step gate? The template ANDs SS_OK into every sequence and init-drive transition but leaves it off states 2/3, 25 (wait for index complete), 124, 99, 127, 1 and 0 — is that a general rule a generated station should follow?
proposedSolution: Yes, and the principle is: SS_OK gates transitions that COMMAND new work (start a stroke, close a gripper, begin an init move). Transitions that merely record that something already finished (init complete 124), that hand control to a partner's handshake (wait-for-index 25), or that are override/protective (lockout 99, fault 127, manual 1, safety 0, idle 2/3) must move regardless of the step button — otherwise a technician stepping the station can hold the machine in a faulted or unsafe state, or stall the dial by never releasing q_StationComplete.
context: single-step / operator debug modes in R02 — from S05_ServoPNP.L5X

question: In dry run, the template makes CycleStationA/B true off DryRun alone, so Attempt/Success latch into a nest that holds no part. Is writing part tracking during dry run intended, or should DryRun imply SingleDisableTracking?
proposedSolution: Intended: dry run is meant to exercise the WHOLE chain — qualification, attempt/success, station performance and the indexer's StationComplete — so that a dry cycle proves the handshakes as well as the motion. The template gives a separate, deliberate opt-out for the cases where the data must stay clean: SingleDisableTracking gates the OTLs and SingleClearTracking COPs an empty part status over the nest. Guidance for generated stations: keep DryRun purely in the two qualification places, keep the tracking-hygiene bits on the OTLs, and clear the nest records before returning the machine to production.
context: dry run vs part tracking — from S05_ServoPNP.L5X R01 rung 25 / R02 rungs 11 and 14
